title: Why your friends have more friends
hook: Pick anyone's friend at random. Surely they are about as popular as anyone else?

doesNotKnow: size-biased sampling: picking through links favours well-connected people

misconception: The average person's friends are about as popular as the average person.
objective: The learner can explain that a person with many friends appears on many friend lists, so a friend picked at random is likely to be well connected: on the five-person star a random friend has 3.4 friends on average against 1.6 for a random person.

claims.text: In the five-person star, the average person has 1.6 friends.
Picking a random person and then one of their friends at random, the friend has 3.4 friends on average.
claims.source: With chance 1/5 you pick the hub and land on a leaf (1 friend); with chance 4/5 you pick a leaf and land on the hub (4 friends): 0.2 x 1 + 0.8 x 4 = 3.4 (meanFriendDegree() in model.ts).

claims.text: Wherever friend counts differ, a randomly chosen friend has more friends on average than a randomly chosen person.
claims.source: S. L. Feld (1991), Why your friends have more friends than you do, American Journal of Sociology 96(6): 1464-1477. Feld's statement is for the mean over friendship links (sum of d^2 / sum of d >= mean d, equality only when all counts are equal); the pick-a-person-then-a-friend average used here is also at least the mean, by a pairing argument: each friendship contributes d_i/d_j + d_j/d_i >= 2.

claims.text: The stage's picks are a seeded sequence; after 101 picks the friend average was 3.32.
claims.source: picks() in model.ts, seed 1991, untuned (the first seed tried). Over seeds 1-500, the average of 101 picks had middle 95% 3.17-3.64 (median 3.41); the minimum was 3.05, always far above 1.6.

claims.text: With the stage's way of picking (a random person, then one of their friends at random), the friend has at least as many friends on average as a random person, with equality only if every pair of friends has the same friend count; so the reveal's "wherever friend counts differ" is strictly true in any connected network but not in, for example, a separate triangle and a separate four-person group where everyone knows all the others.
claims.source: Average = (1/n) x sum over friendships of (d_i/d_j + d_j/d_i) >= (1/n) x 2m = mean friend count, equality iff d_i = d_j on every friendship. Counterexample re-computed in artifacts/scratch/fc-problife/a10b.mjs: triangle + K4 gives 2.571 for both. Added by fact-checker 2026-10-13; needs an independent check.

recall.question: A survey asks random students how big their classes are, and separately asks the school for its average class size. Whose number is bigger?
recall.why: Big classes hold many students, so a random student is more likely to be in a big class: the same bias that makes a random friend more popular than a random person.
